sections.h2: Your options for selling in Cibolo
sections.html:
Three routes are open to a Cibolo owner: list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept cash for the house as it stands. Your repair list and your calendar decide.

  • Agent: the widest audience, but you wait through showings, a buyer's loan and an appraisal.
  • Do it yourself: pricing, negotiation and the contract fall to you.
  • Cash purchase: no repair requests and no loan step, which suits inherited houses, rentals and tight deadlines.

A few Cibolo details shape any route: the city's place east of San Antonio, a county line nearby, and a permit office that works through one online portal.

Cibolo lies in the far western corner of Guadalupe County, along FM 78 and FM 1103, with Interstate 10 to the south and Interstate 35 to the north. It is about 13 miles east of the San Antonio metropolitan area and sits in what the city calls the Metrocom, the northeast corner of Bexar County and the southwest corner of Guadalupe County. Schertz, Universal City, Selma, Live Oak, Garden Ridge, Converse and Kirby are neighbors.

Cibolo voted to become an independent township on October 9, 1965. It counted 440 people in 1970 and an estimated 37,061 in 2023, so many of the lots, surveys and permits you will deal with are recent.

Cibolo is in Guadalupe County, but the surrounding Metrocom reaches into northeast Bexar County. Confirm the tax roll for your parcel on your statement before you set a price.

Valuation happens on January 1 everywhere in Texas, with notices mailed in spring and bills around October 1. A balance still open on February 1 picks up six percent plus one percent interest, then the penalty adds a point each month up to 12 percent in July.

School districts take $140,000 off a homestead, and the home's appraised value can climb no more than 10 percent a year. Your buyer files a fresh application once the sale closes. Call the county tax office for a balance and current rates instead of trusting an online estimator.

sections.h2: Permits and the Cibolo building office
sections.html:
Permits and inspections come from the Cibolo Building and Permitting Department, which wants every application filed in the MGO Connect portal. It is at 201 West Loop 539, and the main office number is (210) 658-4175.

Cibolo building office inspection hours and codes
ServiceHours or rule
Building inspectionsWeekdays, 8 AM through 5 PM
Fire inspectionsTuesday and Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM
Permit portalMGO Connect, account required
Codes in force2021 International codes and 2023 NEC, under Ordinance 1475

Find any permit tied to your address and see whether it was closed. The portal has a permit lookup, and the office email is permitting@cibolotx.gov. A deck, pool, water heater, patio cover or addition that never had a final inspection can stall a title company or a buyer's inspector.

Cibolo enforces the 2021 editions of the International Building, Residential, Energy Conservation, Plumbing, Fuel Gas, Mechanical, Swimming Pool and Spa, and Fire Codes, along with the 2023 National Electrical Code, under Ordinance 1475. Local amendments are listed on the city's Codes and Fees pages.

  • Contractors must register before they submit a permit application.
  • An account in the portal is required before any application.
  • Permits, inspections and permit lookups all run through the same portal.

Before starting repairs, ask the office whether the work needs a permit. If you are selling as-is instead, put any unfinished work in writing for the buyer.

The city's FAQ adds detail for homeowners. Sheds need a permit when they rest on a permanent foundation, can't be moved after installation, or measure over 100 square feet. Water heaters, roof work, replacement HVAC, electrical, plumbing, irrigation and water softener permits can be issued at submittal without plan review. Residential plan reviews may take up to 10 business days, and the city has no process to expedite them.

City Utility Services at Cibolo City Hall, 200 South Main Street, handles water and wastewater accounts, and the city doesn't currently waive deposits or administration fees. Tell your buyer which utility account to open, and close your own as part of the move. Ask the department how much notice it needs for a final reading so you aren't billed after the sale.

If your land was recently annexed, the city's FAQ cites Texas Local Government Code Chapter 43 and lists what changes: voting rights and representation, public street maintenance, land use and density rules through zoning, and code enforcement. An agricultural exemption can continue while the property keeps qualifying, and the city doesn't expect address changes. A buyer of acreage on the edge of town should ask planning staff how zoning treats the parcel.

Texas puts different clocks on each.

  • Probate: a will can be probated for four years after death, and the court has discretion later. An affidavit of heirship may be filed with the clerk, yet a title company can decline it.
  • Tenant: the notice to vacate gives at least 3 days, a justice court case follows, and a writ of possession waits at least 6 days after judgment.
  • Foreclosure: a courthouse auction on a first Tuesday; if the lender later sues for a deficiency, it must do so within two years of the sale.

When two or more of these overlap, a cash buyer can often work around them. Even so, the title company needs documents that show who has authority to sign.

sections.h2: What a buyer will ask about
sections.html:
Expect three questions. Was every permit closed? Which county and appraisal district hold the parcel? Who has authority to sign? Put each answer on paper: the permit record printed from the portal, the tax statement, and the deed, with a payoff letter for any loan and probate papers if an owner has died.

If the property is acreage or was recently annexed, add a fourth: how the city's zoning treats the parcel. Planning staff can answer it before you list, and the buyer will want to hear it from you.

sections.h2: Before you list or take a cash offer
sections.html: Start by looking up your permits and reading your county off the tax statement. Add a payoff figure for any loan. Then decide whether repairs are worth doing or whether to sell as-is and disclose what is unfinished. On closing day, loan and tax payoffs come out of your proceeds, you sign the deed before a notary, and it gets recorded. End your water and wastewater account with City Utility Services once the keys change hands, and let the buyer know which account to open.

faqs.a: The city describes itself as being in the far western corner of Guadalupe County, though its Metrocom area spills into northeast Bexar County. Read your tax statement to learn which appraisal district has your parcel.

faqs.q: How do I check for an open permit on my Cibolo house?
faqs.a: Search the MGO Connect portal, or write permitting@cibolotx.gov, or call (210) 658-4175. Closing out an open permit before you list keeps the sale moving.

faqs.q: Which building codes does Cibolo enforce?
faqs.a: The 2021 International codes plus the 2023 National Electrical Code, by Ordinance 1475. Local amendments are on the Codes and Fees pages of the city website.

faqs.q: When do Texas property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: Anything unpaid at the end of January turns delinquent on February 1, and penalty and interest start building.

faqs.q: Can heirs sell a Cibolo house without a full probate case?
faqs.a: Possibly. When the estate qualifies and a court agrees, a muniment of title or a small estate affidavit may do the job. Ask a probate attorney which one fits.
